parsed_answer.content:
The N+1 problem in GraphQL is a performance anti-pattern that occurs when a client query requests a parent object along with a list of its children, and the underlying data-fetching architecture executes one initial query to fetch the N parent entities, followed by N separate subsequent queries to fetch the children for each individual parent. In a traditional REST API, this issue frequently plagues ORMs like Hibernate when lazy-loading collections without proper joining or fetching strategies. However, in GraphQL, the problem is compounded by the execution model of GraphQL resolvers. Because GraphQL evaluates fields independently using nested resolver functions, a query requesting an author and their books will invoke the book resolver function once for every single author returned by the initial query. If you query 100 authors, the database receives 1 query for the authors and 100 subsequent queries for their respective books, leading to severe network and database I/O latency, connection pool exhaustion, and degraded throughput.

The DataLoader pattern, originally developed by Facebook, is the definitive architectural solution to this problem in GraphQL implementations like DGS or GraphQL-Java. DataLoader introduces two core primitives: batching and caching. Instead of immediately executing a database query inside a field resolver, DataLoader collects all individual keys requested across a single micro-task event loop tick into an array. Once the tick completes, it passes the entire batch of keys to a user-defined batch-loading function, executing a single bulk database query (typically utilizing a SQL 'IN' clause). Furthermore, DataLoader maintains a per-request cache to prevent redundant fetching of the exact same entity if it is requested multiple times within the boundaries of a single GraphQL operation execution.

rows: 2 SQL queries (1 for authors, 1 batched for books)
Extremely high risk of thread/connection starvation

items: DataLoader relies on Java's CompletableFuture to defer execution, allowing the GraphQL execution engine to continue traversing the selection set and accumulating keys into the batch queue.

Batch loading functions must preserve the exact order and correspondence of input keys to output values; if a key has no matching database record, the batch loader must return null or an empty Optional at that specific index.
Request-scoping is mandatory: sharing a DataLoader instance across multiple HTTP requests can cause data leaks where User A accidentally sees cached data belonging to User B.

parsed_answer.content: A classic senior-level pitfall when implementing DataLoaders with Spring Data JPA is assuming that passing a Set of IDs to a repository query automatically avoids database-level performance hits. If your JPA entity mapping still uses FetchType.EAGER or if your IN clause exceeds database parameter limits (e.g., Oracle's 1000-item limit), your batched query will either crash or trigger secondary N+1 issues when Hibernate attempts to hydrate associated relationships. Always chunk your batch keys if your pagination sizes are unbounded.

title: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL? (DataLoader solution)
